implementation_notes: The platform ships the contract: ICommand declares Execute(object), CanExecute(object) and a CanExecuteChanged event, and WPF adds RoutedCommand/RoutedUICommand as ready-made implementations with command binding and input gestures. What the framework does not provide is the inverse - ICommand has no Undo - so an undoable editor keeps a separate do/undo pair (a custom base class or two delegates) beside the interface, and the classic Command class per request is almost never written by hand any more. Outside XAML the whole structure collapses into delegates: Action, Action<T> or a (Action Do, Action Undo) tuple in a List is a complete command history, which is the pragmatic choice for job queues and non-UI invokers.
pitfalls: ICommand has no inverse operation: undo must be layered on with a custom interface or delegate pairs, and pretending Execute is reversible usually ends in a command that guesses state.
CanExecuteChanged subscribers leak UI elements when handlers are never detached; use weak events or a shared CommandManager for long-lived commands.
Delegates capture their target and its fields strongly, so a captured mutable object makes the Undo half restore whatever the value is at undo time rather than at execute time.
